text.hook:
"Lock-free" does not mean "no mutex".
And it does not mean "fast".

The real definition, ABA in one slide, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 📌
text.body:
Inside:
1. The one test that defines lock-free and wait-free
2. The three problems stacked in every lock-free structure
3. ABA, step by step
4. When lock-free is NOT faster

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: is `if (stack.size() > 0) stack.pop();` safe on a lock-free stack? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. size() is only a snapshot: another thread can pop between the check and the pop. Lock-free APIs return the status from the operation itself, e.g. `std::optional<T> try_pop()`.

slides.lead: Not "no mutex". Not "fast". Here is what interviewers actually check.

slides.hero:
Freeze one thread
forever.
Can the others
still finish?
slides.lead: Blocking: no, if it holds the lock. Lock-free: yes, some thread keeps completing. Wait-free: yes, every thread, in bounded steps.

slides.title: Strongest at the bottom
rows: None if a lock holder is delayed
Completes if it runs in isolation
slides.takeaway: Lock-freedom covers the whole path: the atomics (`is_always_lock_free`) and every call, including the allocator.

slides.title: Every lock-free structure must answer

cards.label: 1. CAS
cards.text: Is the shared word still what I based my update on?

cards.label: 2. ABA
cards.text: Did it change away and come back while I was not looking?

cards.label: 3. Reclamation
cards.text: Can another thread still be dereferencing the node I just removed?

slides.takeaway: The CAS loop is the easy 10 percent. ABA and reclamation are where real lock-free code breaks.

slides.title: Start: head -> A -> B -> C
steps: T1 reads `old = A`, `next = B`, then is preempted
T2 pops A, pops B (frees B), pushes A back: head → A → C
T1 resumes: `CAS(head, A, B)` succeeds, head is A as expected
head -> B, a **freed** node. The stack is corrupted
slides.takeaway: CAS compares values, not history. The bug is the cached `next`, computed from a state that no longer exists.

slides.title: ABA and reclamation are different problems
rows: CAS on {pointer, version}. Fixes ABA, **not** use-after-free
Publish the pointer, re-validate. Bounded garbage, a fence per access
Very cheap reads. One stalled thread blocks all reclamation
Readers almost free. Writers wait a grace period
slides.takeaway: Tags answer "did it change?". Reclamation answers "may I free it?" and fixes ABA as a side effect.

slides.title: When lock-free is NOT faster
items: One hot word: every op CASes the same `head`
Retry storms: up to N-1 failed CASes per success
An uncontended mutex is just two atomic RMWs
`new Node` per push may take allocator locks
Hazard pointers cost a full fence per access
slides.takeaway: What it does buy: no stalling behind a preempted holder, no priority inversion, often better tail latency.

items.myth: "Lock-free means no mutex in the code."
items.truth: It is a progress guarantee. A spinlock built from atomics is still blocking.
Only the system does. Progress for every thread is wait-free.

items.myth: "A CAS loop is wait-free because nobody waits on a lock."
items.truth: Unbounded retries make it lock-free only.

items.myth: "Lock-free is automatically faster than a mutex."
items.truth: Often equal or slower in throughput. The win is progress and tail latency.

items.myth: "ABA can be fixed with a timestamp."
items.truth: Use a monotonic version counter inside the CAS word, or safe reclamation.

items.myth: "Check `p != nullptr` before using a popped node."
items.truth: A dangling pointer is not null. `delete` does not touch other threads' copies.

slides.hero:
Lock-free is about
who can stall whom,
not which headers
you include.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
Your ABA-safe stack uses a tagged pointer.
No mutex anywhere in the source. 🧐

Is it really lock-free? Three values decide it.
Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: x86-64, GCC. One of these three values breaks the lock-free claim.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: is std::atomic<int>::fetch_add always wait-free? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: The standard promises no wait-freedom. On x86-64 it is one lock xadd, but on ARMv8.0 without LSE it is an LL/SC retry loop.

slides.title: x86-64, GCC. What prints?

slides.verdict_sub: the 16-byte atomic is not reported lock-free
bullets: The CPU has `cmpxchg16b`, but GCC routes 16-byte atomics through `libatomic` (link with `-latomic`).
So a Treiber stack on `std::atomic<TaggedPtr>` may hide a lock, with no mutex in sight.

slides.title: Fit the CAS word in 8 bytes. Assert it.
bullets: Nodes come from a preallocated pool: 32-bit index + 32-bit tag = one 8-byte CAS.
Or pack the tag into the unused upper bits of a 48-bit pointer (narrower, can wrap).
slides.takeaway: Lock-freedom varies by compiler and flags (`-mcx16`). Make the compiler check it.

text.hook:
"We use only std::atomic, no mutex. So our code is lock-free."

A classic interview question. True or false?
Comment A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜ for the answer.
text.body: The real answer changes how you talk about lock-free code in interviews.

first_comment: 🧠 Follow-up an interviewer would ask next: "This push does `Node* old = head.load(); n->next = old;` once, then loops on `head.compare_exchange_weak(old, n)`. What is the bug?" Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: A failed CAS refreshes old but not n->next, so the retry links n to a stale head and nodes pushed in between are lost. Pass n->next itself as `expected`.

slides.title: Our code uses only std::atomic and no mutex. Is it lock-free?
options: Not necessarily. A thread may still wait on another thread's state.

slides.verdict_sub: Lock-free is about who can stall whom, not which headers you include.
bullets: `while (flag.test_and_set()) {}` is a lock. Preempt the holder and everyone spins.
`new` / `malloc` inside a push can take allocator locks.
slides.cta: Why not A, B or D ➜

items: A: locks can be hand-rolled from atomics, or hidden in library calls.
B: every atomic can be lock-free and the algorithm can still wait.
D: weak vs strong CAS is about spurious failure, not progress.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: "every failed CAS implies another thread's CAS succeeded, and no step waits on another thread's state."

text.hook:
Your lock-free pop's CAS succeeded.
The stack is still corrupted. 🧩

This is the ABA problem. Can you explain it?
Comment A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜
text.body: Slide 2 walks through the exact interleaving, step by step.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: ARM's LL/SC fails if the word was written at all, even back to A. Why can't portable C++ code rely on that to avoid ABA? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: C++ exposes only value-based compare_exchange (x86 has only cmpxchg). Even where it is built on LL/SC, a value that came back to A still matches. Use tags or safe reclamation.

slides.title: Pop reads head `A` and `next = B`, then does `CAS(head, A, B)`. What is the ABA problem?
options: CAS succeeds because head is A again, but the cached `next` is stale.
Nothing: CAS guarantees head did not change since you read it.
Two threads' CASes on head succeed at the same moment.
A memory ordering bug: `seq_cst` on the CAS prevents it.

slides.verdict: A. CAS compares values, not history
slides.verdict_sub: the value went A, then B, then A again
slides.code:
head -> A -> B -> C
T1: old=A, next=B (preempted)
T2: pop A, pop B, free B
T2: push A  => head -> A -> C
T1: CAS(A, B) ok => head = B (freed!)
bullets: The recycled A comes from a node pool, or `malloc` reusing the freed address.
For a plain counter, A to B to A is harmless: nothing hides behind the value.
slides.cta: Why not B, C or D ➜

items: B: CAS only checks equality at the moment of the CAS, not that nothing happened in between.
C: only one CAS wins. The problem is a stale CAS that wins.
D: this interleaving is legal even with `seq_cst`. Ordering does not add history.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: ABA matters when the CAS value stands for more state. Fix it with a version tag, or never reuse a node while it is referenced.

text.hook:
Lock-free stack vs mutex-protected stack.
Which one is faster? 🏁

The obvious answer is the one interviewers wait to correct.
Comment A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: why not just use std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> for the nodes of a lock-free stack? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: It fixes lifetime, but every access pays contended atomic refcount traffic, and atomic<shared_ptr> is usually not lock-free itself.

slides.title: Is a lock-free data structure faster than a mutex-protected one?
options: Yes, always: lock-free code never enters the kernel.
Not necessarily: it buys a progress guarantee and tail latency, not raw throughput.
Yes, especially under high contention on one word.
No, never: CAS retries always make it slower.

slides.verdict_sub: Choose lock-free for its progress guarantee, not for assumed speed.
bullets: Both versions serialize on the same hot cache line.
Lock-free adds failed-CAS retries, allocation and reclamation fences.
An uncontended mutex is just two atomic RMWs, no syscall.
Measured, 4 threads push/pop: both ≈ 20x slower than single-threaded. Lock-free only modestly faster.
slides.cta: Why not A, C or D ➜

items: A: an uncontended mutex does not enter the kernel either.
C: high contention on one word means retry storms. Throughput can fall as threads grow.
D: it often ties or wins modestly, and wins clearly when a mutex holder gets preempted.
slides.takeaway: Senior answer: the bigger win is usually removing sharing (sharding, an SPSC queue per pair). Decide by requirements, measure p50 and p99.
